purpose: This tool lets you move dots on a number line and watch the mean, median and spread react. You learn which number describes a typical value and why one far-away dot can fool the mean.

stops.title: Dots on a number line
stops.text: Each blue dot is one value, stacked when values match. Drag any dot left or right, it snaps to whole numbers from 0 to 20. A yellow triangle marks the mean, a violet dashed line the median, and a green band the standard deviation.
stops.try: Drag the rightmost dot far to the right. Which marker moves most?

stops.title: Add or remove dots
stops.text: Add a point places a new dot at the median. Remove a point takes the last one off. You can have from 3 to 15 dots, then drag to change them.
stops.try: Add a point, then drag it far from the others.

stops.title: Ready-made data sets
stops.text: Symmetric, outlier, wide and skewed load four example sets, and the dots slide into place. Compare how the mean and median agree or disagree in each.
stops.try: Press Outlier, then Skewed. Watch the gap between mean and median.

stops.title: Mean on or off
stops.text: The yellow triangle is the mean, where the dots would balance like a seesaw. Hide it to focus on the median alone. The Median and Standard deviation toggles under it work the same way.
stops.try: Turn off the mean and median, then turn them on one at a time.

stops.title: Standard deviation band
stops.text: A green band centred on the mean, as wide as the typical distance of a dot from the mean. Wide data gives a wide band. Read the number sigma in the readout.
stops.try: Press Wide, then Symmetric, and compare the band.

stops.title: What Next does
stops.text: Each step loads a data set and says what to look for: a symmetric set, an outlier that drags the mean, a wide set with the same mean, and a skewed set.

teacher: Load Outlier and ask students to predict which of mean or median will move before dragging the far dot. Ask: when would you report the median instead? Misconception: that the mean is always the typical value. Show that equal means can have very different spreads.
